name: Power BI
oneLiner: Microsoft's flagship BI and self-service visual analytics platform.
whatItIs: Power BI is Microsoft's business-intelligence platform — the dashboard-and-report layer at the end of the pipeline, and one of the most widely used BI tools anywhere. Analysts build data models and reports in Power BI Desktop, then publish to the Power BI Service (cloud) where users consume them in the browser or Teams. It connects to Synapse, Azure SQL, ADLS and hundreds of other sources, and can either import data into its in-memory engine (VertiPaq) or query live (DirectQuery). Its modelling language is DAX. Power BI is now also the analytics surface of Microsoft Fabric. It's where curated data becomes the reports business users live in.

inPractice.narrative: Data is modelled in Synapse (or Fabric). An analyst connects Power BI, imports key tables into its in-memory model for speed, defines DAX measures, and builds an interactive report. They publish it to the Power BI Service, where colleagues view and slice it in the browser or inside Teams — with row-level security ensuring each region sees only its own data. Power BI is the presentation/serving layer turning warehouse tables into the reports people use daily.

coreConcepts.detail: Power BI Desktop is the free authoring app (model + build reports); the Power BI Service is the cloud platform for publishing, sharing, refresh and governance.
Import loads data into the in-memory VertiPaq engine (fast, needs refresh); DirectQuery queries the source live (current data, load/cost on the source). Composite models mix both.
DAX is the formula language for measures/calculations over a star-schema model; good modelling is what makes reports fast and correct.
Rules restrict which rows each user sees, so one report safely serves many teams, regions or customers.
Shared capacity (Pro per-user) vs dedicated Premium/Fabric capacity (F SKUs) for large models, more refreshes and broad distribution without per-viewer licences.
Power BI is the BI experience within Microsoft Fabric, sitting over OneLake — the direction Microsoft is steering analytics.

whenToUse: Dashboards and reports for business users, especially Microsoft-stack orgs.
Self-service analytics with strong in-memory modelling (import mode).
Live reporting over Synapse/Azure SQL via DirectQuery.
Distributing analytics through Teams/Office and Fabric.
Row-level-secured reports serving many audiences from one model.
whenNotToUse: Heavy data transformation — model/prepare upstream; keep Power BI as the serving layer.
Purely non-Microsoft stacks where another BI tool fits the ecosystem better.
Massive live queries that would overload the source via DirectQuery without tuning.
Governed code-first semantic modelling across tools where a LookML-style layer is required.

keyFacts.label: Authoring
keyFacts.value: Power BI Desktop (free); publish to the Service.

keyFacts.label: Language
keyFacts.value: DAX for measures; Power Query (M) for prep.

pricingShape: Power BI has two main models: Pro is a modest per-user monthly licence (author and share in shared capacity), while Premium Per User or dedicated Premium/Fabric capacity (F SKUs) provides larger models, more frequent refreshes, and — importantly — lets you distribute reports to many viewers without a per-viewer licence. So small teams pay per user; broad enterprise distribution favours capacity-based pricing. Underlying sources (Synapse, Azure SQL) are billed separately, and DirectQuery pushes query cost onto them. Levers: pick per-user vs capacity by audience size, prefer import mode for speed, and tune models.
gotchas: Import mode needs scheduled refreshes — stale data or failed refreshes silently mislead users.
DirectQuery keeps data current but every interaction queries the source, adding load/cost — tune or cache.
Broad viewer distribution needs Premium/Fabric capacity; relying on Pro per-viewer gets expensive.
DAX has a real learning curve; sloppy measures cause wrong numbers and slow reports.
Row-level security must be configured and tested or a shared report leaks data across audiences.

equivalents.name: Amazon QuickSight
equivalents.note: Serverless BI with SPICE caching and pay-per-session viewers.

equivalents.name: Looker
equivalents.note: Governed BI with LookML semantic modelling; Looker Studio is the free lightweight option.
